content: Tormentil, scientifically known as Potentilla erecta, is a herbaceous perennial plant that belongs to the Rosaceae family, commonly referred to as the rose family. It is also known by the name septifoil. This plant is characterized by its low, clump-forming growth habit and slender stems, which can range from procumbent (trailing along the ground) to arcuately upright. The plant typically grows to a height of 10 to 30 cm and produces runners that do not root. Tormentil is native to Asia and northern Europe, where it thrives in a variety of habitats, including forest clearings, meadows, sandy soils, and coastal dunes. Its flowering period extends from May to August or September. The plant produces a single yellow flower, measuring 7 to 11 mm in diameter, which grows at the tip of a long stalk. The flower is notable for its four notched petals, each measuring 3 to 6 mm in length. This four-petaled structure is relatively rare within the rose family. The petals are slightly longer than the sepals, and the flower contains 20 to 25 stamens. The leaves of Tormentil are glossy and pinnately compound. The basal, or radical, leaves are attached to the plant by long petioles, while the leaves along the stems are typically sessile or have shorter petioles. Each leaf is composed of three obovate leaflets with serrated edges. The stipules, which are leaf-like structures at the base of the leaf stalks, are palmately lobed. The plant has a thick rhizomatous root system. The dried root has historically been used to prepare a lotion with medicinal properties. This lotion has been employed to treat various conditions, such as stopping bleeding and alleviating diarrhea. Additionally, the root has been used as a food source during times of scarcity and as a natural dye to color leather red. The plant produces 2 to 8 dry, inedible fruits.
